title: Anyone else nearing release completely blown away by what solo/indie devs did before AI?
author: thatguywithimpact
selftext:
As I get closer to actually publishing my game, the sheer amount of work is hitting me. Even with x100 AI multiplayer for speed it's just crazy.

Looking back at successful indie devs who pulled this off completely without AI tools AND made their game fun... Just massive, MASSIVE respect.

comments.author: Affectionate_Fact854
comments.body:
As someone that did game dev prior to ai 
I'm not blown away with engine based game dev (meaning using godot, unity or unreal engine ) So much


What blows my mind is 
These devs that made stuff like Rollercoaster tycoon 
Sim city 
Diablo 2 
Portal 


Things from early game engine era 
To custom game engine era

replies.author: Mvisioning
replies.body: Roller coaster tycoon is the real alien in the room. So many smart objects moving on screen at once... So much customization...in assembly...

replies.author: Affectionate_Fact854
replies.body:
Yea it's crazy how that guy managed to optimize his game so well(and he was solo dev)
But I mean alot of games from the early era is just mind blowing 

The limited compute (cpu) they had and what they managed to do with bare minimum support besides some programing text books and very small I guess MySpace communities is mind blowing 


That era you had to limit cpu cycles like crazy , spread cpu cycles out over frames and actually carefully place functions containing for loops 

You still do it today , but the fresh hold is Gigs now , not MB

replies.author: jon_cybernet
replies.body:
Rollercoaster Tycoon predates MySpace by almost half a decade. Maybe bulletin boards? Also the dial up web was comparatively expensive to use back then in the UK, and search engines didn’t exist in the same way they do now. So many things we now take for granted just didn’t exist then - social media was still a way off and even Friends Reunited was still a few years away. 

Even since then Chris Sawyer has never had much of an online presence, so I suspect much of his work was done in a vacuum.

comments.author: Strange-Tap5860
comments.body:
Yea people underestimate how hard making games are.

Thats why when I see devs taking 5 years to make a game, or Silksong taking longer, Im just like....yea, that makes sense.

So much of it is just grinding away at a lot of bits - and a lot of bits you hate doing - for years and years.

This is why A.I gamedev is still not going to result in tonnes of new amazing games. They will not have had years of playtesting, polishing, retesting etc. And yea, I get A.I speeds things up again, but you still need it to chip and grind away at lots of small details. It takes perseverance, and it feels like using A.I just increases our urge to kinda....one shot things. Decreases our long term attention span.

comments.author: Maple-Syrup89
comments.body:
Lots of respect. I had only ever coded some basic prototypes for a few games before. 

Before AI, I spent much of my creative game design time making card and board games since I had the skills to do that. 

Coding was the hardest part for me, but that is only about 30% of what makes a game great. Art, sound, motion, camera, lighting, menu UI, dialog, animation, trailer making, marketing, promo, game feel/"juice."  All of that is still required to make something not shovelware.

comments.author: barret232hxc
comments.body: They still do it today lol. The problem is burnout, like I can make a prototype in one day with ai assisted gamedev to test if the game is good. comments.author: AsparagusOk8818
comments.body:
The fact that even one single functional video game exists is, despite my deep well of cynicism, a testament to what humans can and will do. By all rights, such projects should all fail. 

They spend most of their development life being awful; there are long odds of them ever being good once completed, and even longer odds of them finding an audience if they are good.

Why build that? 

Because we can't NOT build it. Because the dream of building it is what winds up the springs in our brains while we sleep.

It's like how KSP 1 teaches not just the how of rocket-building mechanics, but the why of it. 

  
Larian Studios put together a little memento package of their early days that I just look at while listening to music sometimes. A tremendous struggle, and it could have easily all been for nothing.

But instead, the world was gifted with some of the most amazing art of this era.

comments.author: Broudy001
comments.body: Huge amount of respect for solo developers who didn't have Ai.  From my perspective at least Ai reduces the time required for most things for me, gave claude a screenshot of what I wanted my ui to look like, it built it, changed the way the interactions worked from the then current method, to suit the new ui.  Could I have done it yes, but not in the time frame, so my respect for solo devs is sky high they've put so much effort into their projects.

comments.author: adelie42
comments.body:
Yes and...

I am now absolutely infuriated by apps, particularly from big companies with STUPID bugs that someone with half a brain and Claude could hot patch in minutes. I blame the anti-AI crowd because where a thorough adversarial pass could take months (and be nightmarishly boring work) and hundreds of thousands of dollars in man-hour salaries that need to be justified, it can now be done in a few hours and a few million tokens. My tolerance for bugs in production software is virtually non-existant.

To your point more directly, I am still blown away by games that were written in assembly. There were some really great ones, and the idea they were done with essentially no abstraction is incredible.

AI is doing more to prove that given a genie in a bottle most have a really hard time making good wishes; which is what I think all those stories were meant to convey. Success takes hard work. Claude can build your dreams. Can't make you iterate on the depth to take it somewhere.

comments.author: thegalgadev
comments.body: I’m still pretty early in learning game dev, and even small projects have made me appreciate how much goes into getting a game across the finish line. AI can speed up parts of the process, but it can’t make all the polishing, testing, and decision-making disappear. Huge respect to anyone who shipped before these tools existed.

comments.author: Important_Luck_3546
comments.body:
I'm most blown away by game designers.

AI implements things way faster, but it's so freaking hard to make the game fun. I probably did like 12 different prototypes for my game with different angles (roguelike, autobattler, strategy, incremental etc..). It's so easy to whip out a different prototype. Even when in my vision it sounded super cool, after prototyping it I would quickly realize it actually sucks.

Even when you copy the successful formula from an existing game, coming up with the content and then balancing it is so hard, or at the very least time consuming in some mind numbing way.

I think this is the wall that most AI gamedevs will hit and fail overcoming, probably me included lmao.

Oh an also I cannot imagine just working on a game for years. After just a few months of being unemployed even though I have a long runway of savings just the pressure is REAL and when I'm not making progress it SUCKS. Big respect for all the devs who pull through multiyear developments, that must have some pretty hard times.
